extracted.intended_audience: number theorists, computational mathematicians, and PARI/GP users (including people embedding libpari or writing GP scripts)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for installing, configuring, and using the PARI/GP system: choosing kernels, understanding PARI types and precision, GP input language and metacommands, performance tips, and where to get help/bug reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantages of PARI/GP
rubrics_metrics.description: The three main advantages of the system are its speed, the possibility of using directly data types which are familiar to mathematicians, and its extensive algebraic number theory module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PARI/GP is specialized and fast for number-theoretic tasks; it does badly on some symbolic tasks (e.g., multivariate polynomials, formal integration) compared to systems like Magma, Maple, Mathematica. Non-mathematical strengths: programmability (scripting or library), mature development, active mailing lists, developer support, and Free Software licensing (GNU GPL).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ways to use PARI
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI is used in three different ways: 1) as a library libpari called from an upper-level language (C/C++), 2) as the gp programmable calculator whose language GP contains control instructions, 3) via gp2c which translates GP code to C producing much faster code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose library mode for embedding and performance-critical work; use gp as interactive calculator and scripting language; compile scripts with gp2c to run ~3–10× faster and obtain C code that can be hand-tuned or serve as libpari programming tutorial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the tutorial and reference card first
rubrics_metrics.description: A tutorial for gp is provided in the standard distribution and you should read this first. You can then read the more detailed manual. The refcard gives a quick idea of available functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with tutorial.dvi and refcard.dvi/ps for quick orientation; refer to Chapter 3 for complete function descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to report bugs and get support
rubrics_metrics.description: Bugs are submitted online to the Bug Tracking System available from PARI’s home page. The home page also provides sources, binaries, version info, mailing list archives, FAQs and tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the URLs on the PARI home page to submit bugs and consult mailing list archives and FAQs before reporting; follow further instructions on the Bug page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiprecision kernel selection / Portability
rubrics_metrics.description: The PARI multiprecision kernel comes in three non-exclusive flavors: (1) ANSI C version (portable), (2) versions with time-critical parts in inlined assembler for various architectures (ix86, Sparc, Alpha, Itanium, PowerPC, HPPA), (3) a kernel using the GNU MP (GMP) library which improves performance for large operands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ANSI C kernel for portability; enable the GMP kernel if GMP is present (recommended for operands ≳100 decimal digits). See Appendix A for setup and compiler recommendations (gcc preferred). Historical kernels deprecated.

rubrics_metrics.name: License and redistribution requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI/GP is free software under the GNU General Public License (version 2 or later). Permission is granted to make and distribute verbatim copies provided the copyright and permission notice are preserved; modified versions or translations may be distributed under identical permission notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Redistribute only under GPL terms and preserve notices; there is no warranty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types are dynamic, recursive, and can be mixed (with cautions)
rubrics_metrics.description: GP is not statically typed; in library mode all PARI objects are GEN but have internal types. Most PARI types are recursive: components of compound types can themselves be any type. Mixing compatible types is permitted but can lead to nonsensical objects (e.g., 'complex numbers of complex numbers') and unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid creating exotic recursive objects in library mode; expect sensible results only for mathematically meaningful combinations. Be careful mixing reals and modular types (some combinations are disallowed). Consult the type list (t_INT, t_REAL, t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC, t_POL, t_SER, t_MAT, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact vs inexact objects (PARI philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Operations and functions should first give as exact a result as possible, and secondly be permitted if they make any kind of sense. Types t_REAL, t_PADIC, t_SER are imprecise; any object containing these anywhere is inexact. Exact operations between exact objects yield exact results; operations involving inexact objects yield results as precise as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember that mixing objects of different accuracies may discard digits; default precision is only used to convert exact types to inexact ones. Use localbitprec to adapt precision locally rather than changing global defaults too often.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision handling and real/p-adic/series zero semantics
rubrics_metrics.description: Imprecise types carry precision/accuracy and exponents: real zeros have exponents (printed as 0.Exx), p-adic and series zeros are O(pe) or O(X^e). A t_REAL object has an internal precision; 0.E n returns a real zero of exponent n; 0. returns a real zero of default precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use realprecision (decimal digits) or realbitprecision (bits) to inspect/modify global precision; prefer localbitprec in programs for localized precision changes. Beware that numbers smaller than machine epsilon may be treated as exact zero in comparisons/operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automatic mapping of mixed-type operations to a suitable ring
rubrics_metrics.description: When objects of different types are combined they are first automatically mapped to a suitable ring where the computation becomes meaningful (e.g., rational 1/3 mapped to Mod(1/3,5) => Mod(3,5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permissive behavior is convenient but can be surprising: check results when combining modular, p-adic, rational, and complex types. Use explicit conversion functions if you need strict-type behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissive componentwise evaluation of scalar functions
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI usually allows a scalar (transcendental) function to operate componentwise on vectors or matrices — e.g., taking exp of a vector applies exp to each element. For square matrices, PARI assumes componentwise evaluation, so matrix exponential is not the standard matrix exponential unless implemented separately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use apply or explicit loops when needed, but often PARI does the elementwise action for you. For true matrix functions (matrix exponential), implement or use specialized functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior of standard arithmetic operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard operators +, -, *, / exist. Division is, as far as possible, an exact operation (e.g., 4/3 yields (4/3)). Integer/polynomial Euclidean division (\, %) exist; \/ computes quotient minimizing remainder absolute value. Exponentiation ^ applies when exponent is integer; otherwise treated as transcendental. Logical operators !, &&, || return 1 (true) or 0 (false).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of exact rational arithmetic by default; to force floating evaluation use forms like 1./3 or 0.+1/3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversions and type-changing functions available
rubrics_metrics.description: Many conversion functions are available: floor, ceiling, rounding, truncation, real/imag part, conjugation, norm, absolute value, changing precision, creating intmod or polmod, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these to move between representations; many are documented in Chapter 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transcendental functions support
rubrics_metrics.description: Transcendental functions usually operate on complex numbers, power series, and some on p-adics; list includes exp/log, trig functions, modular functions, Bessel functions, polylogarithms. They extend componentwise to vectors/matrices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function availability is expanding; consult extended help (??, ???) or Chapter 3 for complete lists and domain restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetic and factoring functions and guarantees
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic functions explicitly use prime factor decompositions; PARI includes a factoring engine (Shanks SQUFOF, Pollard rho, Lenstra ECM, MPQS) and outputs strong pseudoprimes which may be certified by APRCL.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use built-in factoring routines for integer factorization tasks; for certified primes/certificates use the APRCL test. For heavy factoring, choose appropriate algorithms and parameters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other function areas supported
rubrics_metrics.description: PARI also implements many routines for polynomials (roots, factoring), power series (substitution, reversion), linear algebra (determinant, characteristic polynomial, linear systems), recursions, numerical analysis (univariate integration via double-exponential method), root finding (bracketed), polynomial interpolation, infinite series evaluation, and plotting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chapter 3 for detailed descriptions and examples of these routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance caveat: some types are convenience-only and slower
rubrics_metrics.description: Types t_INTMOD, t_FRAC, t_PADIC, t_QUAD, t_POLMOD, t_RFRAC are provided for convenience, not for speed: they perform reductions after each basic operation and can be inefficient for heavy calculations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For performance-critical code, cancel denominators and work with integers, use homomorphic imaging/modular methods, or program against libpari in C. Example given: rational arithmetic entails gcd computations making it slower; Mod-type arithmetic can be much faster for modular computations.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP startup, defaults, and preferences file (gprc)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start gp with: gp [-D key=val ] [files]. -D key=val sets internal parameter defaults. gp reads a preferences file (gprc) if found, which customizes defaults. Files listed are GP scripts loaded on startup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use -D flags, gprc preferences, or interactive commands to set defaults. The startup banner indicates available features (readline, GMP kernel). Review defaults list in Section 2.12.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting help from gp (metacommands)
rubrics_metrics.description: Type ? to get a menu of function categories; ?n lists commands in category n (corresponding to Section 3.n). ?functionname gives short explanation. ??functionname gives complete description if extended help available. ???"query" lists relevant gp functions. ?. returns available pre-defined member functions. Metacommands start with \ or ? and are not computing commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ? ? ? (single/double/triple) depending on needed detail. Investigate extended help availability; use ?? and ??? when installed with extended help. Use ?\ for metacommand summary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line editing and readline support
rubrics_metrics.description: If gp was properly installed, a line editor (readline) is available offering command-line editing, automatic completions, history navigation. Availability is indicated in the gp banner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If readline is not available, consider reinstalling or consult the person who installed gp. See Section 2.15 for readline commands and Section 2.16 for PariEmacs integration.

rubrics_metrics.name: GP input syntax, semicolon behavior, and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Type expressions and hit Return; a final semicolon suppresses printing of the result (but result still stored in history). Several expressions on one line separated by semicolons form a seq whose value is the last expression and is stored in history. History entries are referenced as %1, %2, ... or shortcuts % and %' etc. The time to compute an entry is stored and accessible via %#.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suppressing output with ; keeps results in history but hides their numbers—prefer assigning to variables rather than relying on history indices. Default history queue length is 5000 (modify with histsize). Use %# to inspect computation times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiline input and brace/continuation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Three ways to continue lines: backslash \ at end of line ignores the newline; newline after an = is ignored (useful in function definitions); braces { } denote a multi-line command where newlines are ignored until closing brace. Braces do not nest and newlines inside { } are concatenated (so newlines should occur after semicolons, commas or operators).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not split identifiers across lines inside braces; avoid programs where concatenation without semicolons produces unintended tokens (example a = b\nb = c becomes a=bb=c). Prefer explicit semicolons and clear formatting to avoid subtle bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupt and quit behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Typing quit at the prompt ends the gp session. Pressing Ctrl-C interrupts the current computation and returns control to the gp prompt, printing a message showing where it was aborted and elapsed time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ctrl-C does not necessarily reflect exact CPU time spent in that function, only that the evaluator was busy processing it. Use interrupts to halt long computations and examine state.
